You will receive content signals from one or more source documents.
Your sole task: classify this course into EXACTLY ONE of the three rule families below.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
RULE FAMILY DEFINITIONS
(read these carefully before classifying — families have overlapping vocabulary)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

insurance_ce — Insurance Continuing Education
  Governed by: State insurance regulatory departments (NAIC, state DOIs)
  Audience:    State-licensed insurance producers, agents, adjusters, back-office staff

  CHOOSE insurance_ce when the content predominantly covers:
  • Property & Casualty insurance: auto, homeowners, commercial property, liability, flood (NFIP/Wright Flood), workers comp, inland marine
  • Life insurance: term, whole life, universal life, variable life
  • Health insurance: individual/group health plans, HMO/PPO, Medicare supplements, long-term care, disability income
  • Employer-sponsored benefits / employer health plans (ACA, COBRA, HIPAA, ERISA) when framed as insurance product knowledge
  • Annuities when the course focuses on insurance licensing, suitability for insurance agents, or state-regulated annuity products
  • Insurance producer licensing, CE credits, state-specific rules (e.g. Washington LTC, Louisiana flood)
  • Coverage, premiums, underwriting, endorsements, policy exclusions, claims handling
  • NAIC guidelines, state DOI regulations, Gramm-Leach-Bliley from an insurance perspective

  KEY SIGNALS: "licensed agent", "insurance producer", "policy", "coverage", "premium",
    "NFIP", "flood zone", "P&C", "homeowners", "workers compensation", "state DOI",
    "CE credit", "state insurance department", "continuing education hours"

  DISTINGUISH FROM iarce: Insurance CE covers insurance products and state licensing.
    If annuities appear alongside securities regulations or FINRA — lean iarce.
    If employer health benefits appear alongside fiduciary / investment concepts — consider iarce.

iarce — Investment Adviser Representative Continuing Education (Ethics & Professional Responsibility)
  Governed by: NASAA / SEC (state and federal securities law)
  Audience:    Investment Adviser Representatives (IARs), registered investment advisers, dually-registered reps

  CHOOSE iarce when the content predominantly covers:
  • Investment adviser regulations: fiduciary duty, RIA registration, Form ADV, investment advisory agreements
  • Ethics and professional responsibility for IARs and advisers
  • Securities law: Investment Advisers Act 1940, Securities Act 1933/1934
  • Behavioral finance, investor psychology, suitability / best-interest standards in investment context
  • Portfolio management, asset allocation, investment strategies as taught to advisers
  • Variable annuities / variable life from a securities regulation angle (not insurance licensing)
  • NASAA model rules, state securities divisions
  • IAR CE requirements (NASAA Series 65/66 context)

  KEY SIGNALS: "investment adviser", "IAR", "fiduciary", "RIA", "Form ADV",
    "NASAA", "Investment Advisers Act", "securities regulations", "suitability",
    "investment advisory", "portfolio", "asset allocation", "behavioral finance"

  DISTINGUISH FROM firm_element: iarce is for IARs and investment advisers under SEC/NASAA.
    Firm Element is for FINRA-registered broker-dealer personnel under FINRA Rule 1240.
    If content covers broker-dealer supervisory procedures or FINRA registered reps — use firm_element.

firm_element — Firm Element Continuing Education
  Governed by: FINRA Rule 1240 (formerly Rule 1250)
  Audience:    Registered representatives (RRs), broker-dealer principals, supervisors, compliance officers, operations staff at FINRA-member firms

  CHOOSE firm_element when the content predominantly covers:

  • FINRA rules and regulations: suitability, best execution, order handling, disclosure

[Heading 1] 1.0 Introduction
Demographers, marketers, and others interested in the U.S. population and its characteristics routinely categorize the population along multiple dimensions, depending on the objective of the study being undertaken. Although there are many more segments or cohorts into which the U.S. population is often divided, the typical demographic variables include age, gender, race, religion, language, etc. It is on the first demographic variable noted, age, that we will spend some time because of its significant impact on the need for long-term care.

[Heading 1] 3.0 The Nature of Long-term Care
For the many accustomed to thinking of long-term care in terms of care provided in nursing homes in which old and frail residents are little more than warehoused as they wait to die, a definition of long-term care is needed. Unlike the foregoing image, long-term care is provided in multiple settings to individuals with a wide range of needs and objectives.

[Heading 2] 3.1 Long-term Care Defined
Long-term care may be provided to the individual who needs minimal assistance in dressing or bathing, or it may involve caring for a patient that requires around-the-clock nursing care. Accordingly, long-term care is generally defined as that assistance required to meet an individual’s physical, mental, and/or emotional needs over an extended period of time, involving personal care and related services provided to people who:

[Heading 3] 3.1.1 Activities of Daily Living
As already noted, the definition of long-term care is couched in terms of activities of daily living. Since the term may not be familiar to everyone, we need to identify the activities included. Although these activities of daily living are generally just what we might expect them to be—the activities people need to perform to get through the day successfully—they are specifically enumerated activities.

[Heading 3] 3.1.2 Cognitive Impairment

[Heading 2] 3.2 Conditions Normally Requiring Long-term Care
Long-term care may be for a relatively short period—rehabilitation following surgery or injury, for example—or may be much more permanent. The temporary situations in which long-term care may be required include:

[Heading 2] 3.3 Types of Long-term Care
Long-term care is often categorized based on its objective and the level of nursing care required to deliver it. Accordingly, long-term care may be:

[Heading 3] 3.3.1 Skilled Care
Skilled care is a type of long-term care that is provided under a doctor’s order by a licensed healthcare professional, such as a physical therapist or nurse. It is usually needed by individuals:

[Heading 3] 3.3.2 Intermediate Care
Intermediate care is similar to skilled care; the difference is that intermediate care is provided on an intermittent basis. Similar to skilled care, intermediate care stresses rehabilitation, its goal being to return function to the patient to enable them to return home.

[Heading 3] 3.3.3 Custodial Care
Custodial care is the most common type of long-term care provided. It is care limited principally to helping individuals perform the activities of daily living. The assistance individuals require to perform ADLs may be needed because of some physical infirmity or condition or because of a cognitive impairment that mandates supervision to ensure the individual does not injure him- or herself or others. While custodial care is less intensive and does not require the high level of healthcare training required of those administering skilled or intermediate care, the individual providing custodial care must have some training in order to properly assist an individual in performing ADLs.

[Heading 2] 3.4 Long-term Care Settings
As may already be apparent, long-term care is not a singular type of care; instead, it is a continuum of care that covers a wide range of services and providers. Because the types of care provided may vary considerably depending on the individual’s need, it is reasonable that the settings in which that care is delivered also vary.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1 Nursing Home Defined
A nursing home is a facility providing long-term care services 24 hours each day performed by or under the supervision of a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, or licensed vocational nurse. It may occupy its own separate building, or it may be a distinct part of another facility such as a wing of a hospital.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.1 Services Provided in Nursing Homes
A nursing home may provide:

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.2 Skilled Care
A nursing home that is a skilled care facility provides skilled nursing care or rehabilitation services to injured, sick or disabled residents. It also provides custodial services that are incident to the skilled nursing care that is its principal focus. Of course, a nursing home providing only custodial care is not a skilled care facility.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.3 Custodial Care
Nursing homes that are custodial care facilities nursing homes are designed to provide a safe environment along with a broad spectrum of services to help meet residents’ medical, physical, and social needs. Services normally provided by custodial care nursing homes include:

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.4 Average U.S. Nursing Home Size
According to the CDC’s 2019 report, there were almost 1.4 million nursing home residents in 15,600 facilities. If you include all forms of long-term care, there were 67,000 providers giving care to approximately 9 million people. The survey advised that provisions of long-term care are constantly changing as new modes, such as assisted living, are developed and as changes in reimbursement alter financial incentives. Projections indicate that the number of Americans needing long-term care will be as many as 27 million by 2050.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2 Alternatives to Nursing Homes
As people generally realize—nursing homes are expensive. Furthermore, they may provide services that many people needing long-term care don’t need. So, it is not surprising that various alternatives to entering a nursing home have emerged.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.1 Assisted Living Facilities
We will see later that the majority of long-term care is delivered both formally and informally in the individual’s home. A nursing home may be an obvious—if not the only—alternative when home healthcare is impractical. A third important alternative to either the individual’s home or a nursing home is an assisted living facility (ALF), which can be seen as a bridge between these two choices.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.2 Alzheimer’s Facilities Meet Alzheimer’s Patients’ Special Needs
Alzheimer’s patients and individuals with senile dementia often require care that is different and more intensive than the care required by other individuals needing long-term care. For that reason, certain alternate care facilities—usually called Alzheimer’s facilities or memory units—are devoted to the care of individuals with these diseases.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.3 Custodial Care Facilities
Not all custodial care occurs in nursing homes or in the individual’s home; much of it takes place in custodial care facilities. While custodial care facilities provide a more formal approach to patient care than is generally encountered in home healthcare, they don’t normally provide the medical services provided by nursing homes; instead, they look to practices outside the facility to provide needed medical services. Just as we found with other types of alternative care, custodial care facilities provide a “bridge” between these two locations in which long-term care may be provided.

[Heading 3] 3.4.3 Community-Based Long-term Care Services
Few people would choose to be in a nursing home or alternate care facility if they had a choice. The majority of people would prefer to retain as much independence as possible—not normally an option in such institutional facilities. However, the option to retain independence is often provided through the use of community-based long-term care services. These services are designed to permit individuals to live independently for as long as their need for care allows. Community-based long-term care services are services designed to enable an individual to delay the need for institutionalization by providing needed services in the community or in the individual’s home.

[Heading 1] 3.0 The Nature of Long-term Care
For the many accustomed to thinking of long-term care in terms of care provided in nursing homes in which old and frail residents are little more than warehoused as they wait to die, a definition of long-term care is needed. Unlike the foregoing image, long-term care is provided in multiple settings to individuals with a wide range of needs and objectives.

[Heading 2] 3.1 Long-term Care Defined
Long-term care may be provided to the individual who needs minimal assistance in dressing or bathing, or it may involve caring for a patient that requires around-the-clock nursing care. Accordingly, long-term care is generally defined as that assistance required to meet an individual’s physical, mental, and/or emotional needs over an extended period of time, involving personal care and related services provided to people who:

[Heading 3] 3.1.1 Activities of Daily Living
As already noted, the definition of long-term care is couched in terms of activities of daily living. Since the term may not be familiar to everyone, we need to identify the activities included. Although these activities of daily living are generally just what we might expect them to be—the activities people need to perform to get through the day successfully—they are specifically enumerated activities.

[Heading 2] 3.2 Conditions Normally Requiring Long-term Care

[Heading 2] 3.3 Types of Long-term Care
Long-term care is often categorized based on its objective and the level of nursing care required to deliver it. Accordingly, long-term care may be:

[Heading 3] 3.3.1 Skilled Care
Skilled care is a type of long-term care that is provided under a doctor’s order by a licensed healthcare professional, such as a physical therapist or nurse. It is usually needed by individuals:

[Heading 3] 3.3.2 Intermediate Care
Intermediate care is similar to skilled care; the difference is that intermediate care is provided on an intermittent basis. Similar to skilled care, intermediate care stresses rehabilitation, its goal being to return function to the patient to enable them to return home.

[Heading 3] 3.3.3 Custodial Care
Custodial care is the most common type of long-term care provided. It is care limited principally to helping individuals perform the activities of daily living. The assistance individuals require to perform ADLs may be needed because of some physical infirmity or condition or because of a cognitive impairment that mandates supervision to ensure the individual does not injure him- or herself or others. While custodial care is less intensive and does not require the high level of healthcare training required of those administering skilled or intermediate care, the individual providing custodial care must have some training in order to properly assist an individual in performing ADLs.

[Heading 2] 3.4 Long-term Care Settings
As may already be apparent, long-term care is not a singular type of care; instead, it is a continuum of care that covers a wide range of services and providers. Because the types of care provided may vary considerably depending on the individual’s need, it is reasonable that the settings in which that care is delivered also vary.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1 Nursing Home Defined
A nursing home is a facility providing long-term care services 24 hours each day performed by or under the supervision of a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, or licensed vocational nurse. It may occupy its own separate building, or it may be a distinct part of another facility such as a wing of a hospital.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.1 Services Provided in Nursing Homes
A nursing home may provide:

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.2 Skilled Care
A nursing home that is a skilled care facility provides skilled nursing care or rehabilitation services to injured, sick or disabled residents. It also provides custodial services that are incident to the skilled nursing care that is its principal focus. Of course, a nursing home providing only custodial care is not a skilled care facility.

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.3 Custodial Care
Nursing homes that are custodial care facilities nursing homes are designed to provide a safe environment along with a broad spectrum of services to help meet residents’ medical, physical, and social needs. Services normally provided by custodial care nursing homes include:

[Heading 3] 3.4.1.4 Average U.S. Nursing Home Size
According to the CDC’s 2019 report, there were almost 1.4 million nursing home residents in 15,600 facilities. If you include all forms of long-term care, there were 67,000 providers giving care to approximately 9 million people. The survey advised that provisions of long-term care are constantly changing as new modes, such as assisted living, are developed and as changes in reimbursement alter financial incentives. Projections indicate that the number of Americans needing long-term care will be as many as 27 million by 2050.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2 Alternatives to Nursing Homes
As people generally realize—nursing homes are expensive. Furthermore, they may provide services that many people needing long-term care don’t need. So, it is not surprising that various alternatives to entering a nursing home have emerged.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.1 Assisted Living Facilities
We will see later that the majority of long-term care is delivered both formally and informally in the individual’s home. A nursing home may be an obvious—if not the only—alternative when home healthcare is impractical. A third important alternative to either the individual’s home or a nursing home is an assisted living facility (ALF), which can be seen as a bridge between these two choices.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.2 Alzheimer’s Facilities Meet Alzheimer’s Patients’ Special Needs
Alzheimer’s patients and individuals with senile dementia often require care that is different and more intensive than the care required by other individuals needing long-term care. For that reason, certain alternate care facilities—usually called Alzheimer’s facilities or memory units—are devoted to the care of individuals with these diseases.

[Heading 3] 3.4.2.3 Custodial Care Facilities
Not all custodial care occurs in nursing homes or in the individual’s home; much of it takes place in custodial care facilities. While custodial care facilities provide a more formal approach to patient care than is generally encountered in home healthcare, they don’t normally provide the medical services provided by nursing homes; instead, they look to practices outside the facility to provide needed medical services. Just as we found with other types of alternative care, custodial care facilities provide a “bridge” between these two locations in which long-term care may be provided.

[Heading 3] 3.4.3 Community-Based Long-term Care Services
Few people would choose to be in a nursing home or alternate care facility if they had a choice. The majority of people would prefer to retain as much independence as possible—not normally an option in such institutional facilities. However, the option to retain independence is often provided through the use of community-based long-term care services. These services are designed to permit individuals to live independently for as long as their need for care allows. Community-based long-term care services are services designed to enable an individual to delay the need for institutionalization by providing needed services in the community or in the individual’s home.
